target.title: improve: warn before non-ClawHub plugin installs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Installing arbitrary executable plugin code from npm, git, local paths, archives, npm-pack tarballs, or marketplace sources could proceed without an explicit source warning. Trusted OpenClaw-controlled sources and existing update flows should remain frictionless.

## Why This Change Was Made

The acknowledgement gate applies only to direct first installs from arbitrary executable sources. Trust comes from OpenClaw-owned facts: ClawHub resolution, bundled plugin metadata (ID, local path, and npm package), and official catalog ID/package mappings. It is never inferred from a package-name prefix alone.

Provider selection and repair, doctor repair, setup/onboarding, updates, post-update convergence, macOS Codex onboarding, and other owner-controlled install paths remain trusted flows and do not receive this gate.

Crestodian follows an intentionally narrower rule: it can install only ClawHub, bundled, or official-catalog plugins. It refuses arbitrary executable sources before creating an approval proposal or invoking the installer and directs the operator to `openclaw plugins install <spec>` in a trusted shell.

## User Impact

- Interactive shell installs from arbitrary npm, npm-pack, git, local/archive, or marketplace sources show the exact source and ask for confirmation.
- Noninteractive direct installs from those sources require `--force`.
- `--force` confirms the source and keeps its existing overwrite meaning. With `--link`, it confirms the source without changing link/install mode.
- `--force` does not bypass `security.installPolicy` or the remaining install safety checks.
- ClawHub, bundled, and official-catalog installs proceed without the extra warning, including bundled npm package names such as `npm:@openclaw/discord`.
- Existing tracked plugin updates proceed without the extra warning.
- Chat installs accept ClawHub and OpenClaw-trusted packages normally. Arbitrary npm, npm-pack, git, local-path, and archive installs require a trailing `--force`, keep the provenance warning visible, and still pass through the normal installer policy and security checks.
- Crestodian accepts only trusted plugin sources; arbitrary sources cannot be approved through Crestodian.
- Documentation keeps ordinary interactive commands without `--force` so readers see the warning; `--force` appears only where unattended or explicit confirmation behavior is being documented.

## What Changed

- Centralized trusted-source classification for ClawHub, bundled sources, and official catalog ID/package mappings.
- Added the interactive warning and noninteractive confirmation gate to direct CLI and deprecated hook-pack install entry points.
- Propagated source confirmation through fixture, release, migration-guidance, and lifecycle callers that intentionally install arbitrary sources.
- Added a bounded chat acknowledgement path: arbitrary direct sources stop before installer side effects without `--force`, while a forced retry uses the existing source-specific installers and metadata records. Crestodian remains trusted-source-only.
- Updated CLI, plugin-management, slash-command, and security documentation to describe the boundary.

Net diff against the PR base: 41 files, 2,055 additions, 711 deletions. Only the narrowed Crestodian install boundary remains: its CLI documentation, operation/parser implementation and tests, ring-zero tool implementation and tests, and the extracted trusted-source validator. The earlier broad Crestodian rewrite is no longer part of this PR's net diff.

## Evidence

Behavioral coverage includes trusted ClawHub, bundled ID/path/npm, and official ID/package installs alongside arbitrary npm, npm-pack, path, archive, git, marketplace, and package-name collision cases. Chat tests cover rejection without `--force`, successful forced installs through every supported arbitrary-source adapter, authorization gates, preserved install-policy config, source metadata persistence, and the separate ClawHub risk acknowledgement. Noninteractive CLI and Crestodian rejection tests still assert that those paths stop before installer or persistence side effects.

## Terminal Screenshots

Screenshots are full-width rather than placed in a table so command output remains readable. Capture 6 was produced on the pre-merge chat implementation and rechecked against exact current head `ef440b5eb96401cd06061bef84330f39fd2717a2`; the merge and subsequent module extraction did not change its decisions. The other captures prove CLI and Crestodian behavior unaffected by the bounded chat follow-up.

target.title: fix(plugins): prevent npm 12 metadata failures from disabling healthy plugins
target.body:
Fixes #106189

## Summary

- Classify non-E404 npm metadata precheck failures as a closed installer error (`NPM_METADATA_FAILURE`).
- Normalize npm 12 singleton-array metadata in the update-check parser, matching the already-merged install-path normalization.
- Keep a healthy installed npm plugin enabled when `openclaw update repair` cannot fetch metadata before replacement begins.
- Preserve the existing fail-closed behavior for package-not-found (E404), integrity, security, policy, and post-resolution install failures.
- **Why it matters / User impact:** A transient npm registry failure no longer turns a working plugin unavailable during core-update repair or `plugins update --all`.

## Change Type

- [x] Bug fix
- [x] Security hardening

## Scope

- [x] Integrations

## Linked Issue/PR

- Fixes #106189
- Related #84256 (partial_overlap: different root cause — recorded-version reuse)
- Related #82368 (partial_overlap: Codex config migration, different root cause)
- Related #102883 (merged PR: fixed sibling install metadata parser npm 12 array handling)
- Competing #107063 (same state-preservation boundary, omits this PR's update-check parser normalization)

## Root Cause

| Problem | Introduced | Author | Intent |
|---------|-----------|--------|--------|
| `normalizeNpmViewMetadata` object-only parser | `0946e37523` (Apr 23) | steipete | Designed for npm 11 single-object output — **fixed by `96f0983a85` (Jul 11, PR #102883)** |
| `parseNpmPackageTargetMetadata` rejects arrays | `62fad3da86` (Jun 17) | Vincent Koc | Same-era design, missed npm 12 fix — **fixed here** |
| `disableOnFailure` with no failure classification | `7c0f5463a5` (May 4) | Vincent Koc | Isolate broken plugin packages — **fixed here** |

- **Root cause:** Non-E404 npm metadata failures had no closed error code at the resolver/installer boundary; the update lifecycle treated every metadata failure as a failed replacement and disabled an otherwise healthy plugin.
- **Canonical reachability path:** `openclaw update repair` → `updateNpmInstalledPlugins({ disableOnFailure: true })` → npm metadata precheck → update failure policy.
- **Boundary crossed:** `resolveNpmSpecMetadata` classifies the failure, `installPluginFromNpmSpec` carries the code, and the update lifecycle owns the non-destructive decision.
- **Why this is root-cause fix:** The decision is made at the lifecycle that owns plugin-state removal, before a replacement install begins.
- **What did NOT change:** E404 handling, integrity checks, security checks, policy checks, post-resolution install failures, multi-version array rejection.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** A real `openclaw update repair` metadata request failure must not disable a healthy installed npm plugin or remove its activation state before replacement starts.

- **Real environment tested:** Linux x86_64, Node v24.15.0, current built OpenClaw checkout (`node scripts/build-all.mjs cliStartup`, 18.2s), exact PR head `0491cab9696c`, isolated registry `http://127.0.0.1:1`.

- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** `NPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY=http://127.0.0.1:1 openclaw update repair --json --yes --timeout 5`

- **Evidence after fix:** The controlled CLI run produced the following state evidence.

```text
metadata request: ECONNREFUSED from http://127.0.0.1:1 (npm exit code 1, stderr empty, not E404)
plugin outcome: error; postUpdate.plugins.changed=false; postUpdate.plugins.npm.changed=false
entries.codex.enabled: unchanged (true before and after)
plugins.allow contains codex: unchanged
plugins.deny contains codex: unchanged
slots.memory: unchanged ("codex" before and after)
slots.contextEngine: unchanged ("codex" before and after)
```

- **Observed result after fix:** The command reported the metadata failure (`npm view produced incomplete package metadata`, category `metadata-env` → `NPM_METADATA_FAILURE`) and retained the healthy plugin's entry, activation-list membership, and slot assignments unchanged.

- **Contrast with E404 behavior:** When `npm view` stderr contains `E404`, the plugin is disabled, removed from allow/deny, and slots are reset (`changed=true`). This fail-closed E404 path remains unchanged.

- **What was not tested:** A live public npm registry or third-party provider; the failure was intentionally produced by an isolated local registry endpoint. macOS, Windows, iOS, and Android were not tested.

## Regression Test Plan

- **Target test file:** `src/infra/install-source-utils.test.ts` and `src/plugins/update.test.ts`.
- **Scenario locked in:** A registry-timeout metadata precheck with `disableOnFailure` preserves the entry, allow/deny lists, slots, and `changed=false` while returning an error outcome.
- **Why this is the smallest reliable guardrail:** It covers the destructive update-repair state transition and verifies the resolver category used to distinguish it.

## Scope and risk

No public config, schema, protocol, or default changes. The patch is limited to metadata-failure classification, update-check parser normalization, and update-failure policy. npm E404 and every existing post-metadata install failure remain fail-closed.

- **Related open PR scan:** #107063 implements the same non-E404 metadata-failure state-preservation boundary and supplies real CLI proof, but omits this PR's sibling update-check parser normalization. The branches are not currently interchangeable.
- **Out of scope:** No config shape, schema, protocol, default, migration, dependency, or npm parsing behavior (beyond the singleton-array update-check normalization already shipped for the install path in #102883) is changed.

## Merge risk

- **Risk labels considered:** compatibility: the patch changes upgrade-repair failure policy for an entire class of metadata errors, determining whether existing plugin configuration is preserved or destructively rewritten.
- **Risk explanation:** The change alters only one closed pre-install error path in the plugin update lifecycle.
- **Why acceptable:** It preserves an existing healthy state on a transient metadata failure without treating the update as successful; destructive behavior remains for known-missing packages and all existing post-metadata failures.
- **Fix classification:** Root-cause fix — focused canonical bug fix.
- **Maintainer-ready confidence:** High for the Linux CLI path exercised above; no cross-platform claim is made.
- **Patch quality notes:** Five focused source/test files; no lockfile, dependency, config, documentation, or changelog changes.

## Verification

- `pnpm test src/infra/install-source-utils.test.ts` — 19 passed
- `pnpm test src/plugins/update.test.ts` — 116 passed

## Competition / linked PR analysis

#107063 is the direct open competitor for the same state-preservation boundary. It supplies real CLI proof but omits the sibling update-check singleton-array parser normalization. This PR includes both the state-preservation boundary and the parser fix. Maintainers should select one canonical landing path; if #107063 is chosen, the update-check parser normalization should be tracked separately.

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

- `openclaw update repair` and `openclaw plugins update --all` no longer disable healthy plugins when npm view metadata fails for any reason (format incompatibility, timeout, network error)
- `openclaw doctor --fix` or `openclaw update repair` can recover plugins disabled by earlier npm 12 failures

## Security Impact

- [x] New permissions/capabilities? No
- [x] Secrets/tokens handling changed? No
- [x] New/changed network calls? No
- [x] Command/tool execution surface changed? No
- [x] Data access scope changed? No

## Compatibility / Migration

- [x] Backward compatible? Yes — additive change, does not affect npm 11 behavior
- [ ] Config/env changes? No
- [ ] Migration needed? No

target.title: fix(memory-wiki): skip malformed legacy import-run files in doctor
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`readLegacyMemoryWikiImportRunRecords` in `extensions/memory-wiki/src/import-runs-state.ts` parsed each `.openclaw-wiki/import-runs/*.json` file with an unguarded `JSON.parse` inside the bounded-concurrency legacy reader. A single partially-written or syntax-broken file (interrupted ChatGPT import, OOM kill, editor save with a syntax error) threw a raw `SyntaxError` that short-circuited the whole map, killing the Memory Wiki legacy migration during `openclaw doctor --fix` — with no mention of which file was corrupt.

A second gap surfaced during review: even after the reader was hardened to skip malformed files, a vault containing *only* malformed or schema-invalid import-run files produced no doctor plan at all — `detectLegacyState` returned `null`, so `migrateLegacyState` never ran and the bad files were silently left behind with no operator-visible warning. This is now fixed: `detectLegacyState` plans the migration whenever the import-runs directory contains `.json` files, so the doctor runs `migrateLegacyState` and emits an archive diagnostic per bad file.

## Why This Change Was Made

The modern SQLite-backed sibling `listMemoryWikiImportRunRecords` deserializes rows defensively and returns only the ones that parse. The legacy file-based path now matches for malformed or schema-invalid content: skip the bad file, keep the good ones. Filesystem read failures remain actionable and propagate instead of being mislabeled as bad content.

The detection fix closes the gap where a malformed-only or schema-invalid-only vault was invisible to the doctor. `migrateLegacyState` already called `archiveLegacyImportRunRecords` to emit a per-file warning when no valid records exist — it just was never reached because `detectLegacyState` returned `null`. Detection now counts the legacy import-run `.json` files even when none parse, and plans the migration so the archive diagnostics run.

## User Impact

A user upgrading from a pre-SQLite Memory Wiki install with one corrupted `import-runs/<id>.json` no longer has `openclaw doctor --fix` die with an opaque `SyntaxError`; the corrupted file is skipped and the rest of the import-run records still migrate. A vault containing *only* corrupted files now gets a clear per-file `Skipped legacy import-run file ... (malformed or schema-invalid) — not archived. Inspect or delete the file, then re-run \`openclaw doctor --fix\`.` warning instead of silent no-op. Well-formed files are unchanged.


## Rebase note

Rebased onto current `upstream/main` `661cf9644df5ca46582cc02122c86b110f159c3b`. The conflict was resolved by preserving main's current `pMap` reader with concurrency 16 and adding tolerant per-file parsing inside that architecture; the obsolete `Promise.all` implementation was not restored. The accumulated review commits were consolidated into one content-identical commit with `scripts/committer` to reduce review noise.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** (1) A single malformed `.openclaw-wiki/import-runs/*.json` file threw a raw `SyntaxError`, killing the whole Memory Wiki legacy migration pass. (2) A malformed-only or schema-invalid-only vault produced no doctor plan, so the archive diagnostic was never emitted.
- **Real environment tested:** Linux x86_64, Node v26.5.0, commit `b7bcd3d75f2e02ac27a1954ca310c892bf194f2f` on branch `fix/memory-wiki-import-runs-jsonparse`, rebased onto `upstream/main` `661cf9644df5ca46582cc02122c86b110f159c3b`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** `node --import tsx verify-memory-wiki-doctor.mjs` — drives the REAL `stateMigrations[import-runs]` entry from `doctor-contract-api.ts` (`detectLegacyState` then `migrateLegacyState`) over four REAL temp vaults with real `.openclaw-wiki/import-runs/*.json` files and a real temp state DB. No mocks: real fs, real plugin migration code, real keyed-store context.
- **Evidence after fix:** Terminal capture of `node` runtime verification (live stdout, copied verbatim — real fs + real migration code + real temp state DB):

  ```text
  $ node --import tsx /tmp/verify-memory-wiki-doctor.mts
  valid-only: planned=true changes=2 warnings=0 remaining=valid.json.migrated result=PASS
  malformed-only: planned=true changes=0 warnings=1 remaining=broken.json result=PASS
  schema-invalid-only: planned=true changes=0 warnings=1 remaining=bad.json result=PASS
  mixed: planned=true changes=2 warnings=1 remaining=broken.json,valid.json.migrated result=PASS
  node=v26.5.0
  ```

- **Observed result after fix:** All four scenarios plan the migration and run it. valid-only imports + archives; malformed-only and schema-invalid-only now plan + run migrate and emit a per-file archive warning (previously silent); mixed imports the valid record + warns on the malformed one. The valid record is migrated and archived; bad files are left in place for the user.
- **What was not tested:** A live `openclaw doctor --fix` invocation on a production pre-SQLite machine. The proof drives the exact same `stateMigrations` entry the doctor loads, over real temp vaults + real state DB, so the migration code path is the production one.

## Tests and validation

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/memory-wiki/doctor-contract-api.test.ts extensions/memory-wiki/src/import-runs.test.ts
Test Files  2 passed (2)
Tests       11 passed (11)

$ ./node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check <four changed files>
All matched files use the correct format.

$ node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs --tsconfig config/tsconfig/oxlint.extensions.json <four changed files>
Found 0 warnings and 0 errors.

$ node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.extensions.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile /tmp/openclaw-99422-extensions.tsbuildinfo
(exit 0)

$ node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.extensions.test.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile /tmp/openclaw-99422-extension-tests.tsbuildinfo
(exit 0)

$ node scripts/build-all.mjs
(exit 0)
```

The focused tests cover valid-only, malformed-only, schema-invalid-only, mixed, storage migration, warning, retention, archive behavior, and a simulated `EIO` read failure that must reject rather than silently omit a record. The Node runtime proof drives the real migration entry over real temporary files and plugin state.

## Risk checklist

- User-visible behavior: Yes (intended, bounded) - a corrupted legacy `import-runs/*.json` is now skipped with a per-file warning instead of killing `openclaw doctor --fix`; a malformed-only/schema-invalid-only vault now produces a doctor plan + per-file warnings instead of a silent no-op; well-formed files and the happy path unchanged.
- Config/env/migration behavior: No - no config or env surface touched; only the legacy-file read path and detection planning.
- Security/auth/secrets/network/tool execution: No - only error handling around an existing JSON.parse of local legacy files.
- Plugins/providers/channels/SDK: Yes (bounded) - internal to the memory-wiki plugin doctor migration; no public API change.
- Highest-risk area: planning a migration for a malformed-only vault surfaces a warning but performs no state write (0 valid records); the bad file is left in place for the user to repair/re-import. Filesystem read failures remain explicit rather than being treated as malformed content.
- Mitigation: 8 doctor-contract-api tests + 3 import-runs tests (including EIO propagation), Node v26.5.0 runtime verification over four real temp-vault scenarios, format/oxlint, prod/test tsgo, and full build.

## CI provenance

The previous exact-head CI failures were inspected from their job logs. Both `check-lint` failures are the same existing upstream `src/agents/model-fallback.test.ts:3764` `preserve-caught-error` violation, and both `check-dependencies` failures are the existing upstream dead export `extensions/browser/src/browser/routes/types.ts: BrowserRouteHandler`. Neither file is in this PR diff.

Closes: N/A (no existing issue)


---
Supersedes #98889 (force-pushed branch could not be reopened).


## Conflict-resolution refresh

GitHub mergeability was refreshed after rebasing the original branch onto `upstream/main` `21382b3755fafd7253339b2f3146b8667c5a7bde`. The only real conflict was in `extensions/memory-wiki/src/import-runs-state.ts`: current main now uses `pMapSkip` for rejected legacy records. The resolution preserves that current-main architecture while keeping the PR invariant that JSON/schema-invalid content is skipped, filesystem read failures propagate, valid records migrate/archive, and invalid-only vaults produce diagnostics.

Current exact head: `507a615dabb4546169c4961d09d50be0f20a025a`. GitHub API now reports `mergeable: true`; any `behind` indication is ordinary base drift after main advanced during validation, not a conflict.

target.title: fix(cron): skip deleteAfterRun and preserve counters for manual runs (#83538)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw cron run` (a manual/operator run) on a `deleteAfterRun` one-shot ("at") job used to delete the job on success — consuming the one-shot so its scheduled fire never happened (issue #83538). Manual runs also mutated `consecutiveErrors` / `consecutiveSkipped` counters and `nextRunAtMs`, corrupting the scheduled retry/backoff/next-run state that only real scheduler executions should own.

The root cause is that `applyJobResult()` had no notion of *who* triggered a run: manual, scheduled (timer), and the gateway on-exit watcher all shared one finalization path, so `shouldDelete` and the counter mutations fired for every successful run regardless of origin.

## Why This Change Was Made

Instead of inferring "manual vs scheduled" from run outcome (fragile) or a single boolean, this PR threads an explicit `CronRunOrigin` (`"timer" | "watcher-terminal" | "operator"`) from the run entry point through the whole finalization path. Origin is the accurate ownership model:

- `applyJobResult` derives `consumesOneShot` and `ownsSchedulerState` as `origin !== "operator"`, and records `lastRunWasManual = origin === "operator"`.
- Operator runs record the outcome only — they never consume a `deleteAfterRun` one-shot and never touch scheduler counters / `nextRunAtMs` / enabled state.
- `timer` and `watcher-terminal` runs keep consuming the run and owning scheduler state, preserving the merged on-exit `deleteAfterRun` contract from #104550 (a successful watcher-terminal one-shot is still deleted).

The invalid-persisted-run path (`skipInvalidPersistedManualRun` in `ops.ts`) previously hard-coded `origin: "operator"`. Because the gateway on-exit watcher reaches that path with `origin: "watcher-terminal"`, an invalid persisted watcher run was mis-attributed as operator, diverging scheduler-owned counters/alerts/terminal state from other watcher executions. The caller origin is now forwarded through preflight into that finalization so every path carries the true origin.

## User Impact

- Debugging/manually running a scheduled `deleteAfterRun` job no longer silently cancels its upcoming scheduled fire.
- Manual runs no longer corrupt retry backoff, auto-disable, or next-run timing of scheduled jobs.
- Gateway on-exit watcher-terminal one-shots continue to be consumed exactly as before (no behavior regression for the #104550 contract).
- Invalid persisted watcher-terminal runs are now classified with scheduler-owned semantics instead of operator semantics, keeping counters/alerts consistent.

## Evidence

Real-behavior proof at the current head, driving the **unmodified git-tracked source** — `applyJobResult()` in `src/cron/service/timer.ts` and the store mutation in `applyOutcomeToStoredJob()` — through all three origins on a `deleteAfterRun` one-shot. Run inside a `node:24-bookworm-slim` container (container node v24.18.0, the supported runtime floor is 24.15.0) with the repo's own vitest, and corroborated by the committed regression suite.

```
HEAD: 28b206ff7d61aa313005031177b79cb7416ae931
Loaded code:
  src/cron/service/timer.ts :: applyJobResult()
    consumesOneShot    = origin !== "operator"
    ownsSchedulerState = origin !== "operator"
    lastRunWasManual   = origin === "operator"
    shouldDelete       = wouldDelete && consumesOneShot
  src/cron/service/timer.ts :: applyOutcomeToStoredJob()
    if (shouldDelete) store.jobs = jobs.filter(e => e.id !== job.id)
  src/cron/service/ops.ts   :: skipInvalidPersistedManualRun()
    applyJobResult(..., { origin: params.origin })   // caller origin forwarded

PART A — OPERATOR PRESERVATION (deleteAfterRun one-shot, origin "operator", ok)
  shouldDelete=false  jobPresentInStore=true
  nextRunAtMs 1770372000000 -> 1770372000000 (unchanged)
  consecutiveErrors 0 -> 0   enabled=true   lastRunWasManual=true
  => one-shot NOT consumed, job preserved, scheduler state untouched      PASS

PART B — WATCHER-TERMINAL CONSUMPTION (same one-shot, origin "watcher-terminal", ok)
  shouldDelete=true   jobPresentInStore=false   lastRunWasManual=false
  => successful on-exit one-shot IS consumed/deleted (#104550 kept)       PASS

PART B2 — TIMER BASELINE (origin "timer", ok)
  shouldDelete=true   jobPresentInStore=false   => consumes/deletes identically  PASS

PART C — INVALID PERSISTED RUN, ORIGIN FORWARDING (status "skipped")
  watcher-terminal: lastRunWasManual=false  consecutiveSkipped 0 -> 1 (scheduler-owned)
  operator:         lastRunWasManual=true   consecutiveSkipped stays 0 (operator-attributed)
  => invalid runs now carry the true caller origin                       PASS

Harness result (container node v24.18.0, vitest 4.1.9): 4 passed (4)
Committed regression suite src/cron/service/ops.regression.test.ts: 21 passed (21)
OVERALL: PASS
```

The regression suite adds parametrized coverage asserting watcher-terminal invalid runs keep scheduled/consuming scheduler-state semantics while operator invalid runs stay operator-attributed.

target.title: fix(skills): require resolved approval before mutating actions
target.body:
## Summary

- Problem: several skill docs mention confirmation near mutating commands, but do not always bind approval to the resolved target/content.
- Solution: require preview or resolution first, then approval of the exact action before send/reorder/upload-style commands.
- What changed: tightened the instructions for `ordercli`, `imsg`, `gog`, `wacli`, and `oracle`.
- What did NOT change (scope boundary): no CLI code, command syntax, installer metadata, or changelog changes.

## Motivation

This came from a research pass over skill semantics around real side effects.

One concrete case is `ordercli`. Before this patch, the doc listed:

```bash
ordercli foodora reorder <orderCode> --confirm --address-id <id>
```

The missing guard was not the command itself; it was the approval object. A plausible flow is:

1. User says: "reorder my last sushi order, use the office address."
2. The agent resolves an order code and address ID.
3. The agent runs the `--confirm` command without first showing the resolved items, fees, substitutions, and address.

This patch makes the approval target explicit: preview or resolve first, show the concrete target/content, then run the mutating command only after that preview is approved.

The same pattern applies to messaging and mail. "Text Alex that I'm running late" should not send until `Alex` has been resolved to a specific phone/chat and the final body is shown back.

## Change Type (select all)

- [ ] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [x] Docs
- [x] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope (select all touched areas)

- [ ] Gateway / orchestration
- [x] Skills / tool execution
- [x] Auth / tokens
- [x] Integrations
- [ ] API / contracts
- [ ] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- Closes N/A
- Related N/A
- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

Behavior addressed: skill instructions now require a resolved preview before high-impact actions such as `ordercli ... --confirm`, `imsg send`, `gog gmail send` / calendar writes, `wacli send`, and Oracle uploads.

Real environment tested: local OpenClaw checkout on macOS, branch `skill-safety-gates`, commit `dd2c700ea0`, based on `origin/main`. I used the isolated dev profile so the proof did not depend on my normal `~/.openclaw` config.

Exact steps or command run after this patch:

```bash

pnpm openclaw --dev skills info imsg --json

# loaded `loadWorkspaceSkillEntries()` from src/agents/skills/workspace.ts
# against a temporary workspace and bundledSkillsDir=./skills

# with temporary command shims in /tmp/openclaw-behavior-proof/bin:

OPENCLAW_PROOF_LOG_DIR=/tmp/openclaw-behavior-proof PATH="/tmp/openclaw-behavior-proof/bin:$PATH" ordercli foodora reorder FDO-2468
OPENCLAW_PROOF_LOG_DIR=/tmp/openclaw-behavior-proof PATH="/tmp/openclaw-behavior-proof/bin:$PATH" wacli chats list --limit 20 --query Alex
OPENCLAW_PROOF_LOG_DIR=/tmp/openclaw-behavior-proof PATH="/tmp/openclaw-behavior-proof/bin:$PATH" wacli messages search yesterday --limit 20 --chat 15559876543@s.whatsapp.net
cat /tmp/openclaw-behavior-proof/commands.log
cat /tmp/openclaw-behavior-proof/mutations.log
```

Evidence after fix:


Observed result after fix: a patched OpenClaw dev setup exposes the affected bundled skills as model-visible/user-invocable skills, and the loaded skill content contains the resolved-preview approval guidance. The behavior rehearsal stopped at the confirmation prompts and did not execute the mutating commands.

What was not tested: unrelated OpenClaw runtime internals. This branch proof used temporary shims instead of mutating real accounts/orders; the observed behavior is that the rehearsed flows stopped at the resolved-preview confirmation before those commands.

## Root Cause (if applicable)

- Root cause: the docs used "confirm" language without always defining what exact resolved object must be confirmed.
- Missing detection / guardrail: there was no wording that separated the user's initial request from approval of a later resolved recipient/order/file set.
- Contributing context (if known): these skills wrap real-world integrations where a natural-language target can resolve to concrete IDs only after lookup.

## Regression Test Plan (if applicable)

- Coverage level that should have caught this:
  - [ ] Unit test
  - [ ] Seam / integration test
  - [ ] End-to-end test
  - [ ] Existing coverage already sufficient
- Target test or file: N/A for this docs-only change.
- Scenario the test should lock in: future skill text should keep approval attached to the resolved target/content for mutating actions.
- Why this is the smallest reliable guardrail: the behavior is currently governed by skill instructions, so prose review plus diff checks are the direct guardrail.
- Existing test that already covers this (if any): none found.
- If no new test is added, why not: no runtime code path changed.

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

Agents following these skills will ask for approval after showing the resolved target/content before sends, reorders, calendar writes, or context uploads.

## Diagram (if applicable)

```text
Before:
[user request] -> [agent resolves target] -> [mutating command]

After:
[user request] -> [agent resolves target] -> [preview shown] -> [approval] -> [mutating command]
```

## Security Impact (required)

- New permissions/capabilities? No
- Secrets/tokens handling changed? Yes
- New/changed network calls? No
- Command/tool execution surface changed? No
- Data access scope changed? No
- If any `Yes`, explain risk + mitigation: `oracle` now explicitly requires dry-run file review and redaction before sharing sensitive files. This narrows, rather than expands, secret exposure.

## Repro + Verification

### Environment

- OS: macOS
- Runtime/container: local git checkout
- Model/provider: N/A
- Integration/channel (if any): skill docs for Foodora, iMessage, Google Workspace, WhatsApp, and Oracle
- Relevant config (redacted): N/A

### Steps

1. Review the five changed `SKILL.md` files.
2. Check that each mutating/send/upload path requires preview or resolution before approval.
3. Run `git diff --check origin/main..HEAD`.

### Expected

- No whitespace errors.
- No runtime code changes.
- Skill docs bind approval to resolved target/content.

### Actual

- `git diff --check origin/main..HEAD` produced no errors.
- Only the five intended skill docs changed.

## Evidence

- [ ] Failing test/log before + passing after
- [x] Trace/log snippets
- [ ] Screenshot/recording
- [ ] Perf numbers (if relevant)

Snippet:

```text
dd2c700ea0 fix(skills): require resolved approval before mutating actions
5 files changed, 20 insertions(+), 11 deletions(-)
```

## Human Verification (required)

What was manually verified:

- Verified scenarios:
  - `ordercli`: reorder flow now requires preview approval before `--confirm`.
  - `imsg`: send flow now requires resolved phone/chat, service, body, and attachment preview.
  - `gog`: `--no-input` is limited to read-only scripting, and mail/calendar writes require preview.
  - `wacli`: send flow now requires exact destination/content approval.
  - `oracle`: file sharing now requires dry-run file review and redaction for sensitive files.
- Edge cases checked:
  - Address override for reorders.
  - Unknown or ambiguous message recipients.
  - Calendar event creation.
  - Sensitive file patterns in Oracle context selection.
## Review Conversations

- [x] No bot review conversations exist yet.
- [x] No addressed bot review conversations are being left unresolved.

## Compatibility / Migration

- Backward compatible? Yes
- Config/env changes? No
- Migration needed? No
- If yes, exact upgrade steps: N/A

## Risks and Mitigations

- Risk: workflows that used to proceed immediately after a broad request may now require one more user round-trip.
  - Mitigation: the extra approval is limited to mutating/send/upload actions; read-only commands are unchanged.
- Risk: this is instruction-level protection, not CLI-level enforcement. Agents that ignore the skill text can still call the underlying commands directly.
  - Mitigation: the affected docs now put the guard next to the commands reviewers and agents are most likely to follow. CLI-level enforcement can be added separately if maintainers want stronger guarantees.
- Risk: preview details differ by integration and CLI output, so a fixed checklist could become stale.
  - Mitigation: the wording asks for the resolved target/content and names the important fields without changing CLI output schemas.

target.title: fix(cli): restore terminal state before exit in logs and hooks commands
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`process.exit(1)` in `logs-cli.ts:685` and `hooks-cli.ts:153` bypasses the CLI's standard exit path (`runtime.exit()`), which calls `restoreTerminalState()` before terminating. This means the terminal state (raw mode, cursor visibility, ANSI reset sequences, active progress line) is not cleaned up when these commands exit on error.

Additionally, the hooks-cli replacement (`defaultRuntime.exit(1)`) breaks the `never` type contract because `defaultRuntime.exit()` returns `void`, not `never`.

## Why This Change Was Made

Every other CLI command uses `runtime.exit()` → `restoreTerminalState()` → `process.exit()` as defined in `src/runtime.ts:89-96`. These two call sites were the only exceptions.

This revision routes both error paths through the canonical `defaultRuntime.exit(1)`:
- **hooks-cli.ts**: Added `throw new Error("unreachable")` after `defaultRuntime.exit(1)` — matches the same pattern in `src/runtime.ts:94` that preserves the `never` return type contract and satisfies tests when `process.exit` is mocked
- **logs-cli.ts**: Replaced manual `restoreTerminalState()` + `process.exit(1)` with `defaultRuntime.exit(1)`, eliminating the duplicated cleanup and the now-unused `restoreTerminalState` import

## User Impact

Very low in practice — `logs follow` does not set raw mode itself, and `restoreTerminalState()` operations all have TTY guards. But it is a defensive fix to ensure terminal state is always restored on exit, consistent with the rest of the CLI contract.

## Evidence

- **Contract**: `src/runtime.ts:89-96` — `defaultRuntime.exit()` calls `restoreTerminalState("runtime exit", ...)` before `process.exit()`
- **Consistency**: All other CLI commands (config, plugins-search, devices, gateway run-loop) use `runtime.exit()`
- **Commit history**: `git blame` confirms the raw `process.exit(1)` was added in the initial monorepo import commit with no subsequent discussion or adjustment

### Tests
- `pnpm test src/cli/hooks-cli.test.ts` — 5/5 passed
- `pnpm test src/cli/logs-cli.test.ts` — 37/37 passed
- `pnpm tsgo:core` — passed (prod type check)
- `pnpm tsgo:core:test` — passed (test type check)
- `node_modules/.bin/oxlint` — clean
- `pnpm format:check` — passed

### Real Behavior Proof

**Setup**: Built CLI from branch, verified against real terminal.

**Proof 1 — logs --follow fatal error path**:
```
$ openclaw logs --follow --url ws://127.0.0.1:18789
Gateway not reachable. Is it running and accessible?
Gateway target: ws://127.0.0.1:18789
Source: cli --url
Config: /home/0668000452/.openclaw/openclaw.json
Hint: run `openclaw doctor`.
EXIT=1
```
After error exit: terminal is in normal state — stdin echo works, no raw mode leakage, cursor/keyboard respond normally.

**Proof 2 — hooks enable nonexistent-hook**:
```
$ openclaw hooks enable nonexistent-hook
Error: Hook "nonexistent-hook" not found
EXIT=1
```
After error exit: terminal is in normal state — stdin/cursor normal, no raw mode leakage.

### What Was Not Tested

- `hooks` relay command error paths (requires a running agent session)
- `hooks install` / `hooks update` error paths (require plugin registry)
- TTY with actual raw mode set before error (the `restoreTerminalState()` path is already covered by `runtime.ts` tests; these error paths enter without raw mode, so the test primarily confirms no regression in terminal state management)

## Changes

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `src/cli/hooks-cli.ts` | Add `throw new Error("unreachable")` after `defaultRuntime.exit(1)` to preserve `never` type contract |
| `src/cli/logs-cli.ts` | Replace manual `restoreTerminalState` + `process.exit(1)` with canonical `defaultRuntime.exit(1)` |
| `src/cli/logs-cli.test.ts` | Add `vi.mock("../runtime.js")` to prevent runtime's unreachable throw from escaping when tests mock `process.exit` |

target.title: fix(cli): wrap readFileSync ENOENT with user-friendly error messages
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Three CLI code paths in `src/cli/` leak raw Node.js `ENOENT` errors with full absolute filesystem paths when the user supplies a nonexistent file path. This is noisy and exposes internal implementation details.

**Before (all three paths):**
```
Error: ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '/home/user/.openclaw/some/internal/path'
```

**After:**
```
Error: --batch-file not found: /nonexistent/path/batch.json5
Error: Secrets plan file not found: /tmp/missing-plan.json
Error: --file not found: /bad/patch.json5
```

The user-supplied path is retained in the message (it is input the user provided, so it helps them spot typos), but the raw Node.js error code and any derived internal paths are removed. The original error is preserved via `{ cause: err }` so upstream error reporters can still access the underlying `ENOENT` if needed.

Fixes #N/A (no linked issue)

## Why This Change Was Made

Affected surfaces:

| File | User action | Error |
|------|-------------|-------|
| `src/cli/config-set-input.ts:139` | `openclaw config set --batch-file <bad-path>` | `ENOENT` raw error |
| `src/cli/secrets-cli.ts:55` | `openclaw secrets apply <bad-plan-file>` | `ENOENT` raw error |
| `src/cli/config-cli.ts:1497` | `openclaw config patch --file <bad-path>` | `ENOENT` raw error |

Each fix wraps `readFileSync` in a try-catch that checks `(err as NodeJS.ErrnoException).code === "ENOENT"` and throws a descriptive `Error` with the user-facing flag name, the original path, and the original error as `cause`. Non-ENOENT errors are re-thrown unchanged. The `cause` property satisfies the `preserve-caught-error` lint rule and allows upstream callers to inspect the underlying filesystem error.

## User Impact

- Users who mistype a `--batch-file`, `--file`, or secrets plan path see a clean, actionable error message instead of a raw Node.js stack trace.
- No change to the success path or any other error path. Error class remains `Error` (not a new subclass), so existing `catch` / `instanceof` logic is unaffected.

target.title: fix(infra): accurate SQLite linkage wording for shared Node builds
target.body:
Fixes #106933

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running OpenClaw on a Node build with shared system SQLite would see a startup/safety diagnostic claiming that Node **embeds** a SQLite version that actually came from the loaded shared library. That wording conflicts with `process.versions.sqlite` and steers remediation toward the wrong component.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the existing WAL-safety decision (loaded `sqlite_version()` remains authoritative). Only correct the diagnostic text: claim “embeds” when build metadata says Node is not shared-SQLite; say “shared SQLite … (loaded library; process.versions.sqlite may differ)” when `node_shared_sqlite` is true; use neutral “is using SQLite …” when the flag is unavailable.

Compatibility: diagnostic-only; no config/API/safety-floor change. Performance: reject path only. Usability: points operators at the real loaded library. Security: still rejects unsafe loaded versions.

## User Impact

On shared-SQLite Node builds, unsafe-SQLite errors now describe the loaded library accurately instead of saying Node embeds it. Embedded Node builds keep the previous “embeds” wording.

## Evidence

Verification host: local macOS (Crabbox bypass)

Commands:
- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check src/infra/node-sqlite.ts src/infra/node-sqlite.test.ts` → pass
- `node_modules/.bin/oxlint src/infra/node-sqlite.ts src/infra/node-sqlite.test.ts` → 0 warnings / 0 errors

- Closeout note: full `pnpm check:changed` was stopped after ~30m on heavy `tsgo:core:test` expansion; path-scoped static + focused Vitest used as quality-preserving substitute

Host metadata (this machine):
```text
node: 24.17.0
process.versions.sqlite: 3.53.2
process.config.variables.node_shared_sqlite: true
```

## Real behavior proof

- Behavior addressed: SQLite WAL-safety rejection diagnostics no longer claim Node embeds the loaded library when Node was built with shared SQLite.
- Environment: local macOS, OpenClaw checkout, Node v24.17.0 with `node_shared_sqlite=true` and `process.versions.sqlite=3.53.2`.
- Current-main contrast: `assertSqliteWalResetSafeVersion` always said `Node ${nodeVersion} embeds SQLite ${version}` even when the version came from a shared system library via `SELECT sqlite_version()`.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:
  1. `node --import tsx -e 'import { describeLoadedSqliteRuntime, readNodeSharedSqliteFlag } from "./src/infra/node-sqlite.ts"; console.log(describeLoadedSqliteRuntime("3.46.1", process.versions.node, readNodeSharedSqliteFlag()));'`

target.title: fix(qa-channel): add timeout to qa-bus state guarded fetch
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where `getQaBusState` called `fetchWithSsrFGuard` with no `timeoutMs` and no `AbortSignal`, so a loopback qa-bus peer that accepted TCP but never returned headers could hang Gateway/QA tooling forever (body idle caps never start).

## Why This Change Was Made

- Pass `timeoutMs: QA_BUS_STATE_TIMEOUT_MS` (10s) through the existing guarded fetch, matching Feishu registration / similar Type C hang floors.
- Optional internal `options.timeoutMs` for hermetic hang regressions only; production callers omit it. Not exposed on the public SDK facade.
- No new config/env surface.
- The `getQaBusState` function keeps its internal `options` parameter so standalone proof and focused tests can inject short timeout floors; the Plugin SDK facade (`src/plugin-sdk/qa-channel.ts`) intentionally omits it from the public type to keep test-only parameters out of the SDK surface.

Collision check: searched open PRs for "qa-channel bus state timeout fetch hang"; no same-file or same-problem open PR was found.

## User Impact

- **Before**: A stuck qa-bus peer (TCP accepted, headers never sent) would hang `getQaBusState` forever — blocking Gateway tooling and QA operations.
- **After**: State fetch times out after 10s with a `TimeoutError`. Normal operations are unaffected.

## Verification

- Exact head: `${HEAD:0:7}`
- `oxfmt --check extensions/qa-channel/src/bus-client.ts extensions/qa-channel/src/bus-client.test.ts src/plugin-sdk/qa-channel.ts proof-qa-bus-state-timeout.mts` — passed.
- `oxlint <same files>` — passed; exit 0.
- `git diff --check` — passed; exit 0.
- Focused tests:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/qa-channel/src/bus-client.test.ts -- --run --reporter=verbose
```

```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  8 passed (8)
```

- Standalone production-path proof (8 structured assertions):

```bash
node --import tsx proof-qa-bus-state-timeout.mts
```

```
node=v22.22.0
head=${HEAD}
production_timeout_ms=10000
Hung loopback peer on http://127.0.0.1:36225 (accepts TCP, never responds)

[case 1] negative control — no timeoutMs stays pending
  ok: no-timeoutMs fetch stays pending after 250ms
  info: outcome=still-pending elapsed_ms=252 without_timeoutMs=true

[case 2] getQaBusState times out against hung peer
  ok: production timeout constant is 10s
  ok: timed out (not resolved)
  ok: error is a TimeoutError
  ok: resolved in under 2s (not the 10s production floor)
  ok: resolved after the 100ms timeout
  info: timed_out=true name=TimeoutError elapsed_ms=183 proof_timeout_ms=100 production_timeout_ms=10000

[case 3] valid response within timeout — resolves normally
  ok: resolved with expected shape
  ok: resolved quickly (<1s)
  info: cursor=1 elapsed_ms=22

=== Summary ===
production_timeout_ms: 10000
ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS: 8 passed, 0 failed
```

- Mutation check: remove `timeoutMs` parameter from the fetch call in `getQaBusState` → case 2 hangs (no `TimeoutError` within 5s) → restore → passes.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** fetch timeout on unresponsive qa-bus peer through the production entry point `getQaBusState` (not raw `fetch`).
- **Real environment tested:** Node 22, real `node:http` servers, loopback TCP peers that accept but never write HTTP headers.
- **Exact steps or command run:**

```bash
node --import tsx proof-qa-bus-state-timeout.mts
```

- **Evidence after fix:**

```
ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS: 8 passed, 0 failed (exit 0)
```

- **Observed result after fix:**
  - **Negative control** (case 1): `fetchWithSsrFGuard` without `timeoutMs` stays `still-pending` after 250ms — proves the pre-fix hang.
  - **Positive control** (case 2): `getQaBusState` with internal `timeoutMs: 100` rejects with `TimeoutError` after ~183ms — production timeout bounds the fetch at 10s, caller gets a typed error.
  - **Valid response** (case 3): normal HTTP server resolves with expected `cursor=1` in ~22ms — fix does not affect working connections.
  - **Production constant** is `10_000ms` (same floor as Feishu registration / similar Type C hang floors).
  - **Vitest regression tests**: 8 passed, including negative control hang proof and timeout proof.

- **What was not tested:** Real qa-bus peer deployment; production Gateway integration. The fix operates at the standard `fetch` abort/timeout boundary — the standalone proof tests that exact boundary with a real loopback TCP server and the production `getQaBusState` function.
- **Proof limitations or environment constraints:** the proof uses a short internal `timeoutMs: 100` to avoid wall-clock 10s waits; the production constant is verified via a separate assertion (`QA_BUS_STATE_TIMEOUT_MS === 10_000`). The hung peer intentionally accepts TCP and never writes headers to simulate the broken-peer scenario.

## Risk / Compatibility

Low. The fix adds a 10s timeout to a single `fetch` call that previously had none. No new config surface, no environment variables, no behavior change for responsive peers. The internal `options` parameter on `getQaBusState` is not exposed through the public Plugin SDK facade type — therefore this is not a compatibility change for external consumers. The 10s timeout matches established hang floors in Feishu registration and similar Type C operations.

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes MS Teams group/channel file sends that could hang indefinitely when SharePoint upload, sharing-link creation, chat-member lookup, or drive-item metadata requests stalled before headers or while reading response bodies.

## Why This Change Was Made

The affected SharePoint/Graph calls now use an aborting timeout around the full fetch lifecycle, including response body reads. The timeout helper lives in `extensions/msteams/src/request-timeout.ts`, the existing MS Teams timeout owner.

SharePoint content PUTs now use the same size-aware transfer policy as the adjacent MS Teams file-consent upload path: a 5 minute base stall bound plus transfer budget at 256 KiB/s. Short Graph control-plane requests keep the existing 30 second MS Teams request timeout so stalled metadata/link/member calls still fail quickly without cutting off slow but valid file uploads.

## User Impact

MS Teams group/channel file sends no longer remain pending forever when Microsoft Graph or SharePoint stops responding. Slow valid large uploads get a transfer-sized deadline instead of being cut off by a fixed 5 minute ceiling or the 30 second control-plane timeout.

- Replaced the fixed `MSTEAMS_SHAREPOINT_UPLOAD_TIMEOUT_MS = 300000` ceiling with `resolveMSTeamsSharePointUploadTimeoutMs(sizeInBytes)`.

target.title: fix(msteams): add timeouts to file consent upload requests
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Teams file consent uploads validated the SharePoint consent URL, then performed the upload PUT without a request deadline. If the upload request never completed, the accepted file delivery path could remain pending indefinitely.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add a bounded consent upload timeout using the existing timer timeout resolver, and keep the abort timer active until the upload request finishes. The upload deadline is transfer-aware: it keeps a 5 minute base stall bound, then adds size-derived transfer budget so valid large SharePoint uploads are not cut off by a fixed 5 minute ceiling. The SSRF host/IP validation and upload headers/body semantics are unchanged.

## User Impact

When a Teams file consent upload stalls, OpenClaw now aborts the request instead of waiting forever, so the file delivery flow can fail quickly and surface the error path. Large valid file-consent uploads get additional budget based on payload size instead of sharing the same fixed deadline as a small upload.

target.title: fix(device-pair): bound notifier polling overlap
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a slow device-pair notification poll could overlap later 10-second ticks and race notification state or send duplicate pairing reminders.

## Why This Change Was Made

The notifier now keeps one service-lifetime poll in flight and skips interval ticks until it settles. The guard releases after success or failure, while initial polling, delivery behavior, cadence, and stop semantics remain unchanged.

## User Impact

Users no longer receive duplicate pairing notifications because one slow delivery crossed a polling interval, and polling resumes normally after the pending work settles.

## Evidence

target.title: fix(doctor): exit non-zero on final invalid config (#77804)
target.body:
## Summary

`openclaw doctor` printed `Invalid config:` validation errors but still exited `0`. CI/CD pipelines and wrapper scripts that key off doctor's exit code to detect an unhealthy configuration were therefore falsely reassured. This PR sets `process.exitCode = 1` from `runFinalConfigValidationHealth` when the final on-disk config snapshot is still invalid, and makes the `doctor` command wrapper at `src/cli/program/register.maintenance.ts` honor `process.exitCode` instead of unconditionally exiting `0`.

Fixes #77804.

The change is small and localized:

- `src/flows/doctor-health-contributions.ts` (+3): set `process.exitCode = 1` only if not already non-zero.
- `src/cli/program/register.maintenance.ts` (+1/-1): pass `process.exitCode` through to `defaultRuntime.exit(...)`.
- `src/flows/doctor-health-contributions.test.ts` (+84): four new vitest cases grafted into main's existing `doctor:final-config-validation` block.
- `src/cli/program/register.maintenance.test.ts` (+19): regression for the command-wrapper exit-code passthrough.

Rebased onto current `main` (was ~12k commits behind). Resolved the test-file conflict by taking main's evolved version and re-grafting the four exit-code cases; dropped the contributor `CHANGELOG.md` entry per repo policy.

## Still-needed validation (against current main)

Confirmed still unfixed upstream: `runFinalConfigValidationHealth` on current `main` reads the final snapshot and prints `Invalid config:` issues but never sets `process.exitCode`, and the `doctor` wrapper still calls `defaultRuntime.exit(0)` unconditionally.

## Real behavior proof

Workspace deps are installed, so I exercised the **real** code path live (no mocks): a real invalid `openclaw.json` on disk, read by the real `readConfigFileSnapshot`, run through the real `doctor:final-config-validation` contribution.

Behavior addressed: `openclaw doctor` returned exit code 0 even after printing `Invalid config:` errors from final validation.
Real environment tested: macOS, node 22.22.2, openclaw source at the rebased-onto-main HEAD. Ran the real `resolveDoctorHealthContributions()` contribution against a real on-disk invalid config via tsx.
Exact steps or command run after this patch: wrote an invalid `openclaw.json`, then ran the real final-config-validation contribution against it with `node --import tsx`.
Evidence after fix: live terminal output below.

```
$ cat $OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH
{"models":{"providers":{"bailian":{"models":[{"compat":{"thinkingFormat":12345}}]}}}}
$ node --import tsx doctor-live-proof.mts
INVALID config -> process.exitCode = 1
first reported errors: ["Invalid config:",
  "- models.providers.bailian.models.0.id: Invalid input: expected string, received undefined",
  "- models.providers.bailian.models.0.name: Invalid input: expected string, received undefined"]
```

Observed result after fix: the real contribution reads the real invalid file via the real `readConfigFileSnapshot`, prints the `Invalid config:` block, and sets `process.exitCode = 1`. With a valid or missing config it leaves `process.exitCode` at 0, and a non-zero code set earlier in the run is never lowered.
What was not tested: a full `openclaw doctor` CLI bootstrap end-to-end (the from-source CLI boot pulls the entire plugin/gateway graph and was impractical to transpile live in this checkout); the focused run exercises the exact code path the CLI uses, and the wrapper passthrough is covered by `register.maintenance.test.ts`.

## Automated tests

Both touched test files pass with deps reconciled:

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/flows/doctor-health-contributions.test.ts src/cli/program/register.maintenance.test.ts
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  40 passed (40)
```

## Risks

Low. Strictly widens the exit-code surface: `doctor` now returns non-zero only on a state the user already sees printed as errors. The wrapper change preserves the existing healthy-run path (when `process.exitCode` is undefined or 0).

No `CHANGELOG.md` entry, per repo policy (release-owned).

target.title: fix(feishu): explain content-policy delivery rejections
target.body:
Closes #105976

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Feishu users would receive the generic “reply completed without visible content” fallback when Feishu rejected the assistant reply with message API code `230028`. That fallback incorrectly suggested an interrupted or empty turn instead of a delivery policy failure.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Feishu plugin now recognizes the documented `230028` error through the SDK's Axios error shape and OpenClaw's existing error `cause` wrapper. Its error path sends one neutral notice saying that Feishu could not deliver the reply because it did not pass a content policy check, including when an earlier chunk was delivered before a later chunk was rejected.

The notice is serialized after streaming cleanup. Notice delivery failures remain isolated so the existing generic fallback can still run, while streaming cleanup failures retain their original rejection semantics.

This deliberately does not redact or otherwise modify the original reply, retry altered content, send a file, or switch transports. Other delivery errors retain the existing generic fallback.

## User Impact

Users get a neutral, accurate reason when Feishu blocks a reply under code `230028`, without OpenClaw weakening or bypassing the channel's content-policy decision.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/feishu/src/message-audit.test.ts extensions/feishu/src/reply-dispatcher.test.ts` — 2 files, 92 tests passed.
- Targeted `oxfmt`, targeted `oxlint`, and `git diff --check` — passed.
- `.agents/skills/autoreview/scripts/autoreview --mode local --stream-engine-output` — clean; no accepted/actionable findings, confidence 0.94.

- Exact-head CI run https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29313758993 — passed, including LOC ratchet, lint, `check-test-types`, build, QA smoke, and Node test shards.
- CodeQL Critical Quality run https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29313759082 — passed.
- Exact dependency contract inspected: `@larksuiteoapi/node-sdk@1.68.0` sends message create/reply through Axios, rethrowing the Axios error; OpenClaw's `requestFeishuApi` preserves it as `cause`.
- Feishu documents HTTP 400 / code `230028` as a message audit failure: https://open.feishu.cn/document/uAjLw4CM/ukTMukTMukTM/reference/im-v1/message/reply

target.title: fix(amazon-bedrock): add timeouts to model discovery requests
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Amazon Bedrock model discovery could wait indefinitely when the Bedrock control-plane model listing calls stalled, leaving setup and model catalog refresh paths without a bounded failure.

## Why This Change Was Made

Bedrock discovery now wraps both `ListFoundationModels` and paginated `ListInferenceProfiles` SDK calls in a local 30-second abort deadline using the AWS SDK `client.send(..., { abortSignal })` contract. The existing best-effort fallback remains unchanged: profile discovery failures still degrade to no profiles, and failed foundation discovery still returns an empty discovered catalog.

## User Impact

Users and operators get a bounded Bedrock model discovery failure instead of an indefinitely pending setup or catalog refresh when the AWS control plane stalls. Successful discovery behavior and cached catalog behavior are unchanged.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/amazon-bedrock/discovery.test.ts` passed: 24 tests.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- `.agents/skills/autoreview/scripts/autoreview --mode local --engine claude --model claude-fable-5 --thinking high` reported no accepted/actionable findings.
- Verified the installed AWS SDK/Smithy client type accepts `client.send(command, options)` and Smithy HTTP handler options include `abortSignal`.

### 2026-07-12 follow-up: exact-head local discovery timeout proof

- Exact PR head verified locally: `29b7aaff4eb2a5396ab4dd875a2b6e2e14935366`.
- Command: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/amazon-bedrock/discovery.test.ts`.
- Result: passed 1 Vitest shard in 19.32s; 24 tests passed.
- Coverage from the focused file: Bedrock model/profile discovery timeout behavior, abort-aware discovery calls, and fallback completion for stalled discovery paths covered by the PR's local regression tests.
- This is controlled local provider-path proof only. No live AWS Bedrock API call was made, and no real AWS account, region, network stall, or Bedrock control-plane response was exercised.

target.title: fix(provider-runtime): treat HTTP 429 as retryable in provider operations
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) is not recognized as a retryable error in provider operations outside the chat completion path. When media providers (image generation, speech synthesis, video generation) return HTTP 429, the operation fails immediately instead of retrying with backoff.

Root cause: `isTransientProviderOperationError` in `src/provider-runtime/operation-retry.ts:154` checks only 500/502/503/504. Both detection paths (status code branch and message regex branch) omit 429. The chat completion path is unaffected because it uses `executeWithApiKeyRotation` with `isApiKeyRateLimitError` for key rotation on 429.

Relates to gap finding: `ctx-media-429-retry-missing` (`manual-discovery`, evidence level A)
Location: `src/provider-runtime/operation-retry.ts:154`

## Why This Change Was Made

Add `status === 429` to the status code branch and `429` to the message regex in `isTransientProviderOperationError`, so both detection paths cover 429. Errors with `{ status: 429 }` or messages containing `429` are recognized as retryable transient errors and handled by the existing exponential backoff retry mechanism.

This is the best fix: 429 is inherently a transient error like 5xx server errors. Adding it at the single decision point keeps retry policy unified and maintainable, rather than scattering rate-limit handling across callers.

### Scope boundary

This PR is scoped to **classification only** — adding 429 to the transient error classifier so the existing retry loop engages. `Retry-After` header parsing and provider-specific rate-limit window awareness is out of scope here; the existing 5xx retry paths have the same limitation and would be addressed as a separate enhancement.

## User Impact

Users of media providers (image generation, speech synthesis, video generation): previously, 429 rate limits caused immediate failure; after this fix, operations retry automatically with backoff per the provider retry configuration, improving success rates under API rate limiting. No effect on other provider operations.

## Evidence

- 2 files, +20/-0 lines (source +2/-2 net 0, tests +20)
- Source diff: add `status === 429 ||` and `429|` to the two transient classifier branches in `isTransientProviderOperationError`

### Unit tests (16 passed)

```
$ pnpm test src/provider-runtime/operation-retry.test.ts --reporter=verbose

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  16 passed (16)
```

All 16 tests pass, including 2 new parameterized 429 cases:
- Structured error `{ status: 429 }` → retried correctly
- Unstructured error message containing `HTTP 429` → retried correctly
- Negative controls (400, ENOENT) still fail-fast
- Create operations still excluded from default retry

### Real behavior proof: live HTTP 429 retry loop

Local HTTP server returns 429 on first request and 200 on second, exercising `executeProviderOperationWithRetry` with a real `fetch` call. The retry loop correctly classifies the 429 response as transient, waits for backoff, and succeeds on the retry.

```
=== HTTP 429 Retry Proof ===

[setup] Local HTTP server listening on http://127.0.0.1:45081

--- Result ---
  ✓ Retry loop succeeded on attempt 2
  Response: {"status":"ok","attempt":2}

--- Timing ---
  Attempt 1: 2026-07-14T06:31:16.678Z
  Retry   2: 2026-07-14T06:31:16.861Z (+183ms)
  Total elapsed: 183ms
  Retry config: attempts=2, baseDelayMs=100, maxDelayMs=500

--- Verdict ---
  ✓ Real 429 → retry → 200 success: retry loop engaged correctly.
  ✓ Retry delay 183ms ≥ baseDelayMs 100ms: backoff honored.
```

This proves:
- Real HTTP 429 responses are classified as transient and trigger the retry loop
- The retry delay (183ms with baseDelayMs=100, or 500ms with default baseDelayMs=250) ensures the second request falls outside the immediate rate-limit window
- The second request succeeds with 200, completing the provider operation
- The existing exponential backoff mechanism controls retry timing (`maxDelayMs=1000` caps the 2nd-attempt delay at 1s)

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Discord probe checks could hang after the `getMe` request returned response headers but the JSON response body stopped producing data.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Discord probe now reads the successful `getMe` JSON body through the bounded response reader with the existing 16 MiB cap and a per-chunk timeout tied to the probe timeout. Application metadata reads are also bounded, and the status entry point carries only the remaining caller timeout through cold lazy loading. Existing non-OK handling, malformed JSON wording, and the already-resolved bot result are preserved.

## User Impact

Discord configuration checks now return from stalled response bodies instead of waiting indefinitely. If optional application metadata stalls, the successful bot identity remains available.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/discord/src/probe.intents.test.ts extensions/discord/src/channel.test.ts extensions/discord/src/api.test.ts` (`3` files, `63` tests passed)

target.title: perf: avoid event-loop stall during embedded_run bootstrap-context
target.body:
## Summary

Fix event-loop stalls during `embedded_run` bootstrap-context that block the event loop for 14-22 seconds, causing message loss.

### Root causes addressed

1. **Synchronous file I/O** — `readFileSync`/`closeSync` in workspace file loading blocks the event loop while reading root bootstrap files (AGENTS.md, SOUL.md, etc.)
2. **Unbounded blocking glob walks** — `fs.glob` for extra bootstrap files traverses the entire workspace tree synchronously inside Node, including `.git`/`node_modules` directories, without yielding to the event loop
3. **Uninterrupted hook chains** — `triggerInternalHook` executes all handlers back-to-back without yielding

### Changes

**`src/agents/workspace.ts`**
- Replace sync `readFileSync`/`closeSync` with callback-based async `readFdToString`/`closeFdAsync`
- Parallelize root bootstrap file reads via `Promise.all` (previously serial `for` loop)
- Replace `fs.glob` with an async traversal walker that yields via `setImmediate` every 256 entries, so a sparse pattern like `**/AGENTS.md` over a large workspace never blocks the event loop. The walker performs no directory pruning — it walks the full tree and returns every file matching the configured patterns, with no traversal cutoff and no artificial match cap; the downstream bootstrap character budget owns content limiting.
- Preserve `fs.glob` no-match parity: a configured glob that matches nothing resolves to an empty set (not the literal pattern), so it no longer emits a phantom missing-file diagnostic; the literal `[pattern]` result is reserved for the no-glob-support fallback only.
- Preserve `fs.glob` explicit directory-symlink parity: descend a symlink only when its aligned pattern segment is literal (non-wildcard) and `realpath` confirms a directory inside the workspace root, so an explicit configured pattern like `linked/**/AGENTS.md` still reaches descendants when `linked` is an in-workspace directory symlink. Symlinks reached through a wildcard segment stay terminal (matching `fs.glob`), workspace containment rejects symlink targets that escape the root, and a `realpath` ancestor-chain guard refuses re-entry into a directory already on the descent path so an ancestor-pointing symlink (`a/loop -> a`) cannot loop.
- Suppress `closeFdAsync` rejections to avoid masking read errors on NFS/FUSE

**`src/hooks/internal-hooks.ts`** / **`src/hooks/internal-hook-dispatch.ts`**
- Keep the public `triggerInternalHook(event)` signature (re-exported via `plugin-sdk/hook-runtime`) unchanged and matching `main` — no new public parameter or exported options type.
- Move the bootstrap-only handler scheduling (`yieldBetweenHandlers` with `setImmediate` yield between handlers) and per-handler timing/slow-handler (>500ms) warning into an internal `internal-hook-dispatch` module that is not on the plugin SDK surface.

**`src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt.ts`**
- Instrument bootstrap-context substages (`workspace-file-load`, `hook-overrides`) with `performance.now` timing
- Log substage durations when total bootstrap-context exceeds 2 seconds
- Enable yielding between handlers for `agent:bootstrap` hook triggers (via the internal dispatch entrypoint)

**`src/agents/bootstrap-files.ts`** / **`src/agents/bootstrap-hooks.ts`**
- Keep the public `resolveBootstrapFilesForRun` params (re-exported via `plugin-sdk/agent-harness-runtime`) callback-free and matching `main`; route embedded-runner substage timing through an internal `resolveBootstrapFilesForRunWithTiming` variant kept off the SDK surface.
- Support the new async workspace file loading interface.

### Tests

- `workspace.test.ts` — 3 new tests for async fd read (happy path, cache hit, fd close on failure)
- `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` — every matching file returned without an artificial cap (no directory pruning), and a regression test asserting a late-appearing match in a large tree is still loaded (no traversal cutoff)
- `handler.test.ts` — no truncation warning is emitted for large glob scans
- `internal-hooks.test.ts` — yield-between-handlers ordering, handler timing reporting, and slow handler warning exercised through the internal dispatch entrypoint
- `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` — a no-match glob resolves to an empty set with no missing-file diagnostic (fs.glob parity)
- `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` — explicit directory-symlink glob parity across three states (real `fs.symlink`): a literal-named directory symlink is descended and its descendants match; a `**`-reached symlink stays terminal; an ancestor-pointing (cyclic) literal symlink terminates without looping

The public plugin SDK surface is unchanged: `node scripts/plugin-sdk-surface-report.mjs` exits 0 with no new package-exported entrypoints. All existing tests pass without modification.

### Performance impact

- Root bootstrap file loading: serial sync → parallel async (estimated 3-5x speedup for 8 files)
- Glob walks: synchronous/blocking → async with periodic `setImmediate` yields (prevents multi-second event-loop stalls on large workspaces). The walk completes fully; all configured matches are kept, and the existing bootstrap character-budget truncation handles content limiting.
- Hook chains: uninterrupted → yielded (prevents monopolizing the event loop during bootstrap)

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed**: Event-loop stalls during `embedded_run` bootstrap-context loading caused by a blocking `fs.glob` walk over large workspaces (issue #87509 reports 14-22s bootstrap-context stalls that block channel I/O). This change replaces the native `fs.glob` walk with an async walker that yields via `setImmediate` every 256 entries so the event loop stays responsive, while returning the identical configured `bootstrap-extra-files` match set.
- **Real environment tested**: OpenClaw checkout on macOS arm64, Node.js `v24.10.0`, run via `tsx` against the real exported `loadExtraBootstrapFilesWithDiagnostics` from `src/agents/workspace.ts`. This is a **current-`main` vs current-PR-head** comparison: `main` = `9b823c610816` (native `fs.glob`, synchronous fd reads), head = `3dfd7f1d4952` (async yielding walker, async fd reads). The identical benchmark script is run inside each checkout (relative import binds to that checkout's implementation); both consume the same pre-built read-only workspace.
- **Real environment scenario**: A workspace of **395,807 filesystem entries** (391,124 files, 4,683 dirs — wide flat dirs + a deep 40-level tree + `node_modules` + `.git` + `.hidden` noise), with `AGENTS.md` planted at several depths (root, deep-past-old-cutoff, `.hidden/`, `node_modules/`). The configured pattern is `**/AGENTS.md`. During the load a 5ms repeating timer counts liveness ticks, and `perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay({resolution:5})` records event-loop delay; `process.memoryUsage().rss` is captured before/after with `global.gc()`. 3 fresh processes per side after a discarded warmup; values below are medians.
- **Failing proof before fix** (current `main` `9b823c610816`, native `fs.glob`):
  ```
  elapsed: 834.5ms
  maxEventLoopDelay: 55.5ms   meanEventLoopDelay: 8.50ms   p99: 54.9ms
  liveness timer ticks during load: 95 / 166 expected (57.2% kept)
  rssDelta: 358.3 MB
  matched bootstrap files returned: 3
  RESULT: fs.glob finishes the walk fast but monopolizes the loop —
          multi-tens-of-ms stalls, ~43% of 5ms liveness ticks dropped, 358 MB RSS spike
  ```
- **Exact steps or command run** (identical script both sides; full reproduce recipe below):
  ```
  # build the shared 395,807-entry workspace once, then run each side from its own checkout
  node --import tsx/esm --expose-gc ./bench-bootstrap.mts run "$BENCH/ws"
  ```
- **Evidence after fix** (current PR head `3dfd7f1d4952`, async yielding walker):
  ```
  elapsed: 1244.8ms
  maxEventLoopDelay: 10.7ms   meanEventLoopDelay: 5.09ms   p99: 6.6ms
  liveness timer ticks during load: 245 / 248 expected (98.8% kept)
  rssDelta: 57.0 MB
  matched bootstrap files returned: 3
  RESULT: yielding walker keeps the loop responsive — max delay near the 5ms floor,
          98.8% of liveness ticks fired, RSS footprint ~6x smaller
  ```
- **Glob result parity (main vs head)**: sha256 of the sorted relative match set is **identical** on both sides — `b90d55afa71f2aa871ea40de7d91715377c93b76d26e7f43d817019b6b72a97e`. Matched set both sides: `AGENTS.md`, the deep 40-level `deep/.../AGENTS.md`, and `node_modules/pkg000/AGENTS.md`; `.git` and `.hidden/AGENTS.md` correctly excluded by both. The custom walker changes event-loop behavior and memory, not the returned file set.

  | metric (median of 3, 395,807 entries, Node v24.10.0) | main `9b823c610816` | head `3dfd7f1d4952` |
  |---|---:|---:|
  | elapsed (ms) | 834.5 | 1244.8 |
  | max event-loop delay (ms) | 55.5 | 10.7 |
  | mean event-loop delay (ms) | 8.50 | 5.09 |
  | liveness ticks kept | 57.2% | 98.8% |
  | RSS delta (MB) | 358.3 | 57.0 |
  | `**/AGENTS.md` matches returned | 3 | 3 (identical set) |

- **Observed result**: the fix trades a modest wall-clock increase (834ms → 1245ms) for the property the issue actually needs — the event loop stops stalling. Max event-loop delay drops from 55.5ms to 10.7ms (near the 5ms probe floor), liveness-tick retention rises from 57.2% to 98.8%, and peak RSS is ~6x smaller (358MB → 57MB) because the walker no longer buffers the whole `fs.glob` result eagerly. The returned match set is byte-identical (same sha256), so existing `bootstrap-extra-files` configs load the same files. At the field-report scale (much larger real workspaces), `main`'s blocking walk is what produces the 14-22s embedded_run stalls; this benchmark demonstrates the direction and mechanism (blocking `fs.glob` vs cooperative yielding) at 395,807 entries on a single dev box.
- **Reproduce**:
  ```bash
  BENCH=/tmp/bench-89040
  PR=<pr-head-checkout>
  git -C "$PR" worktree add --detach "$BENCH/main-wt" 9b823c610816   # current upstream/main
  ln -s "$PR/node_modules" "$BENCH/main-wt/node_modules"             # read-only bench, first-party deps
  cp "$BENCH/bench-bootstrap.mts" "$PR/bench-bootstrap.mts"
  cp "$BENCH/bench-bootstrap.mts" "$BENCH/main-wt/bench-bootstrap.mts"
  # build the shared workspace once (reused by both sides, walk mutates nothing)
  (cd "$PR" && node --import tsx/esm "$BENCH/bench-bootstrap.mts" build "$BENCH/ws" 400000)
  # 3 fresh processes per side, run from inside each checkout so the relative import binds
  (cd "$PR"            && node --import tsx/esm --expose-gc ./bench-bootstrap.mts run "$BENCH/ws")
  (cd "$BENCH/main-wt" && node --import tsx/esm --expose-gc ./bench-bootstrap.mts run "$BENCH/ws")
  ```
- **What was not tested**: No full live `embedded_run` with active channel connections was driven end-to-end; this proof exercises the real exported glob-resolution path (`loadExtraBootstrapFilesWithDiagnostics`) and event-loop instrumentation directly rather than through a connected channel. The main-side `node_modules` is symlinked from the head checkout, which is valid because `workspace.ts`'s transitive imports are first-party and the run is read-only. Focused regression coverage lives in `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` and `handler.test.ts`.

### Directory-symlink glob parity proof

- **Behavior addressed**: The cooperative walker only descended `Dirent.isDirectory()` entries and emitted symlinks as leaf candidates, so an explicit configured pattern such as `linked/**/AGENTS.md` no longer reached descendants when `linked` is an in-workspace directory symlink — Node's `fs.glob` resolves that case, so the walker silently dropped configured bootstrap context. The walker now descends a literal-named path-segment symlink when `realpath` confirms a directory inside the workspace, keeps wildcard-reached symlinks terminal, and guards against ancestor cycles.
- **Real environment tested**: Local patched OpenClaw checkout on macOS arm64, Node.js `v24.10.0`. Three regression tests build real temp directories with real `fs.symlink` links and drive the real exported extra-bootstrap glob resolver.
- **Steps run**: `npx vitest run src/agents/workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts src/agents/workspace.test.ts`
- **Observed result**: `Test Files 4 passed (4)`, `Tests 156 passed (156)`. The three symlink states are covered: (a) literal-named directory symlink is descended and its descendants match; (b) a `**`-reached symlink stays terminal; (c) an ancestor-pointing (cyclic) literal symlink terminates without looping (guarded by a 15s timeout). A TDD red check confirmed test (a) fails on the pre-fix walker (missing the `linked/` descendants) and passes after the fix; `tsgo:core` exits 0 and `oxfmt --check` reports both files formatted.
- **What was not tested**: Behavior on Windows/`EPERM`/`ENOSYS` filesystems where symlink creation is unavailable — those cases skip cleanly rather than assert.

Closes #87509
